articles.title: A 104-year-old woman finally received her brother's World War II dog tag 83 years after his death; the long-lost identification has now made its way back to the family
articles.summary: A 104-year-old woman in Massachusetts has received her brother's military identification tags 83 years after he died in a plane crash during World War II.
articles.body: A 104-year-old woman in Massachusetts has received her brother's military identification tags 83 years after he died in a plane crash during World War II. Dorothy Stewart, who was 21 when her brother Bernard Parnell died in 1943, was reunited with his dog tags at a ceremony held at a YMCA last month.According to CBS Boston, the identification tags were found among old military records at Beverly Veterans' Services. Officials did not know how they had reached the office, but spent several years trying to locate Parnell's surviving family members. Their search eventually led them to Stewart, who was still living in Beverly.For Stewart, the discovery brought back memories of her brother, whose body was never recovered after the aircraft crashed off the Florida coast. Speaking to CBS Boston, she recalled his appearance and popularity when he was young. "First off he was handsome. The girls used to chase him all of the time," she said.The reunion became possible through the efforts of Ken McKay, assistant director of Veterans' Services in Beverly. He had been examining old records when he discovered the tags. A document submitted more than five decades earlier eventually helped him identify Stewart and arrange their return.How Bernard Parnell died Bernard Parnell joined the US Navy following the Japanese attack on Pearl Harbor in December 1941. He subsequently travelled to Florida, where he was training to serve as a radioman aboard an aircraft.His life ended in 1943 when the aircraft developed engine trouble and crashed into the sea off Florida. Stewart remembered what she had been told about the incident, including her brother's actions before the crash. "It had engine trouble and it crashed off the coast of Florida," she said.According to Stewart, Parnell gave a life jacket to the aircraft's pilot, Lieutenant James Digh. The pilot survived the crash, but Parnell did not. "The pilot was the only survivor. My brother's body was never found," Stewart said.With his remains never recovered, the family had no opportunity to bring him home. His military identification tags were also missing for decades, until their discovery among the records maintained by Beverly Veterans' Services.Discovering the missing tagsThe search began when McKay was going through a collection of historical documents stored in a tote at the veterans' services office. Some of the records dated back to the Spanish-American War.Among the documents were several military identification tags belonging to former service members. Parnell's tags were part of that collection. "This is the fourth or fifth maybe dog tag that we've pulled out of these files," McKay told CBS Boston.McKay could not establish how the tags had originally reached the office. Nevertheless, he began looking for relatives who might still be alive.For approximately four to five years, the tags remained hanging on a frame in his office while he continued his research. According to People magazine, McKay would investigate available records, put the search aside when he reached a dead end and return to it later.As more historical documents became available digitally, he was able to make progress. One record proved particularly useful- an application for a headstone for Bernard Parnell, submitted in 1972. The person who had filed that application was Dorothy Stewart.How McKay found StewartFinding Stewart's name was an important development, but McKay initially doubted whether she would still be alive. Given the number of years that had passed since the headstone application, he began by searching for her obituary. "Due to her age, I initially just searched for an obituary," he said.Instead, McKay came across a news article about Stewart's achievements in indoor rowing. She had won five consecutive world championships while competing in an age category she described as 95 plus.The rowing article gave McKay a possible way to contact her. He approached the YMCA, explained his position and told staff why he wanted to reach Stewart. "With that, I called the YMCA, and explained who I am. They thought I was a scammer at first," McKay recalled.The YMCA eventually helped establish contact, allowing McKay to arrange the return of the identification tags.An emotional reunion after 83 yearsOn September 29, Stewart attended a ceremony at the YMCA, where her brother's dog tags were formally returned to her. The Beverly Veterans' Council had placed the tags in a frame before presenting them.Receiving the tags brought an emotional response from Stewart, who had lived for more than eight decades without her brother. "I broke down and cried. I just held it after I kissed it. Who would have dreamed after all of this time?" she said.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Chinese woman buys around 200 parking spaces in bulk, charges double the original rent and wins legal battle with neighbours
articles.summary: A Chinese woman’s decision to buy nearly 200 parking spaces in a residential complex has turned an investment bet into a bitter dispute with her
articles.body: A Chinese woman’s decision to buy nearly 200 parking spaces in a residential complex has turned an investment bet into a bitter dispute with her neighbours. Wu spent 14 million yuan, around US$2 million, on the spaces when demand was low, expecting the surrounding area to develop. As the neighbourhood grew and parking became more sought after, she began renting and selling the spaces at higher prices. However, residents who struggled to find affordable parking challenged her ownership in court, sparking a debate over private property rights and access to essential residential facilities.Why did a Chinese woman’s parking space investment spark a legal feudAccording to the South China Morning Post (SCMP), Wu bought 196 parking spaces in a residential development in Changsha, Hunan province, in a single transaction. The purchase represented 40% of the project’s total parking inventory.The Star, in its report, also highlighted how the woman’s plan to resell the spaces for profit angered residents and led to legal action. The development’s name was not disclosed in the reports.The dispute began with a decision that initially appeared to be a calculated business move. Instead of purchasing a few spaces for personal use, Wu invested heavily when the property market in the area was struggling. Her neighbours, meanwhile, became concerned when the spaces they needed were increasingly controlled by one owner.The disagreement eventually moved beyond the question of whether Wu could make money from her purchase. It became a conflict over whether a single investor should be able to control such a large share of a residential community’s parking supply.Wu grabbed an opportunity when others stayed awayThe SCMP reported that the residential project was completed and put on the market in 2018. At the time, the neighbourhood lacked essential amenities, including shops, schools and convenient public transport. Many potential buyers were sceptical about its prospects, and demand for both homes and parking spaces remained weak.Wu took a different view after examining regional development plans issued by local authorities. She believed the area would grow and decided to invest while the developer was facing serious financial difficulties.The developer agreed to sell her the 196 spaces for 14 million yuan, approximately US$2 million. Her decision involved a substantial financial commitment, but it also meant acquiring a large share of the available parking before demand increased.As anticipated, the surrounding area developed, homes in the complex sold more quickly and demand for parking rose. The investment that had looked uncertain during the project’s early days consequently became a source of potential income.She committed her money when others were hesitant, but the resulting ownership concentration later became the central source of friction with residents.What made the parking spaces a source of conflictAccording to The Star, Wu installed parking locks to prevent people from using her spaces without permission. She began renting some of them for 500 yuan, around US$75, per month, roughly twice the rental price originally set by the developer in 2018.Residents asked her to reduce the monthly rent to 300 yuan, but she declined. She later listed spaces for sale at around 100,000 yuan, or US$15,000, each, with some asking prices reportedly reaching 80% above their original values.For residents who needed parking, these prices presented a problem. They believed the spaces should be available at the original rates, particularly because parking was an everyday necessity.A government official was sent to mediate between Wu and the residents, but the effort failed to settle the dispute. An undisclosed number of residents subsequently joined forces to challenge the purchase in court.Their argument was that parking spaces formed an important part of the residential community’s infrastructure and should not be monopolised by someone seeking to profit from resale. They asked the court to annul the contract between Wu and the developer.The court ruling favoured Wu’s right to own the spacesThe legal challenge reached a decisive point in February 2024, when a local court in Changsha ruled in Wu’s favour, according to The Star.The court noted that residents had been given the opportunity to purchase parking spaces when the developer initially offered them for sale. They had chosen not to buy them, whereas Wu had committed her money and accepted the financial risks.The court also found that no law restricted the number of parking spaces an individual could own. It therefore considered Wu’s bulk purchase legal and rejected the residents’ attempt to invalidate the original contract.Although Wu’s ownership caused widespread dissatisfaction within the community, the court’s reasoning centred on the original sale and the absence of a legal limit on individual ownership.The case continues to divide public opinionThe SCMP reported that the dispute attracted renewed attention on Chinese social media in late September 2026. Reactions reflected the divide between people who considered Wu a shrewd investor and those who believed parking should primarily serve the needs of residents.Some online users supported her, arguing that the developer had offered the spaces to residents before she bought them. Others questioned whether it was fair for one person to control so much parking while neighbours struggled to find affordable spaces.The court ruling settled the legal challenge to her purchase, but it did not remove the underlying disagreement. For Wu, the spaces represented an investment made with her own money. For her neighbours, they represented access to convenient and affordable parking.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: Owls ringed to measure impact of Purbeck's nature-friendly farming
articles.summary: A barn owl and 15 chicks are ringed to see if conservation-focused farming is working.
articles.body:
Barn owl chicks have been ringed in Purbeck for the first time to help track their movements and if the area's conservation-focused farming is working.

The 15 chicks and one adult were ringed at nest sites across three farmland sites in a partnership between Birds of Poole Harbour, Carey Ringing Station and the National Trust.

Mark Singleton, Purbeck's National Trust countryside manager, said: "This is an exciting project and a first for us in Purbeck. Although barn owl numbers have fallen significantly over the past century, there are encouraging signs they may be recovering locally."

Set to run every year, the project hopes to expand with more nest boxes put up next year.

Singleton said National Trust tenant farmers were managing the land to support wildlife with areas of longer grass, maintaining hedgerows and patches of scrub.

He said: "These habitats support the voles and other small mammals that barn owls rely on.

"By monitoring ringed birds over many years, we'll be able to assess how effective these measures are and continually improve what we're doing."

Kate Fox, licenced bird ringer and ornithologist from Carey Ringing Station, said: "Ringing provides invaluable scientific data about these birds, which can't be gained from observations alone.

"Barn owls are striking birds, but it's very difficult to tell individuals apart. If birds move to a different nest box, we won't know whether it's a new pair or birds we've recorded elsewhere unless they have been ringed."

The ringing was carried out under a special licence and follows strict guidance from the British Trust for Ornithology (BTO).

Barn owls are a Schedule 1 breeding species, meaning it is illegal to disturb them during the breeding season without a licence.

articles.body: The probe into the flydubai stabbing incident has widened as two Maldivian pilots were also detained just 3 days after Omani copilot attacked Indian pilot Smit Machchhar on September 30.The two Maldivian pilots were detained in UAE on October 3, as per PTI quoting Maldivian news portal Adhadhu. Their identities have not been revelaed publicly, however, their families have been formally informed by the Maldivian Embassy in the United Arab Emirates. Additionally, there has been no confirmation on this development by the authorities.The arrests come as authorities investigate the alleged links of the two men to the accused co-pilot, Omani national Hammam al-Hammami.According to Maldivian newspaper Mihaaru (cited by PTI), the two pilots are believed to have interacted with al-Hammami at their workplace and lived in the same building as him. However, authorities have not officially disclosed the nature of their alleged links to the incident or the evidence against them.The two are reportedly among six Maldivian nationals working as pilots for flydubai and are reportedly the airline's most recent recruits from the Maldives.The incident involved flight FZ1073, which was carrying 174 passengers and crew members from Dubai to Tel Aviv. Al-Hammami, 29, allegedly attacked the flight's pilot, Indian national Machchhar, with an axe and stabbed him in an attempt to seize control of the aircraft and carry out what the UAE has described as a "terrorist attack".Despite sustaining serious injuries, Machchhar resisted the alleged assault and managed to unlock the cockpit door. Crew members and passengers then entered the cockpit, overpowered the co-pilot and helped stabilise the aircraft. The plane subsequently made an emergency landing at Tabuk airport in Saudi Arabia.UAE authorities have said al-Hammami was suspected of supporting extremist ideologies and that Omani authorities had previously barred him from obtaining a pilot's licence. Investigators are examining how he was recruited by flydubai despite the reported restriction, along with the motive behind the alleged plot.The UAE Attorney General has said a comprehensive investigation is underway in coordination with regional security agencies to establish the circumstances of the incident and determine whether al-Hammami had links with other individuals or groups.Meanwhile, in India, the National Investigation Agency (NIA) registered a case last week to probe the alleged mid-air attack and uncover the larger conspiracy behind it. The case has been registered under the Anti-Hijacking Act and the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act, bringing the incident under the purview of India's anti-terror investigation agency.MEA had earlier said Machchhar was responding well to treatment after undergoing surgery at a hospital in Abu Dhabi. articles.summary: Germany's Nuremberg Airport temporarily suspended flight operations on Tuesday after police received a report of a suspected aviation emergency shortly
articles.body: Germany's Nuremberg Airport temporarily suspended flight operations on Tuesday after police received a report of a suspected aviation emergency shortly before a flight from the Greek island of Corfu was due to land.The aircraft landed safely, but operations remained suspended as police secured the airport and investigated the incident, according to Reuters."We received a report of an unclear air emergency," police said in a statement on X. Investigations into the cause are currently underway."An airport spokesperson confirmed that the plane had landed safely and that Eurofighter jets had accompanied it before landing, dpa reported. The suspected emergency had not been confirmed, a police spokesperson said.According to The Express, the flight was operated by Corendon Airlines and was expected to arrive at around 12.15 pm (local time).Flight-tracking service Flightradar24 showed that the aircraft landed at 12.16 pm (local time).Possible drone sighting reported overnightThe latest disruption followed reports of a possible drone sighting near the airport overnight.Bavarian police said three pilots had independently reported seeing an object during take-off or landing procedures between 2 am and 4 am local time on Tuesday.Border police, airport management and German air traffic control launched measures to investigate the reports and locate the object.A police helicopter was also deployed, but officers were unable to verify the sighting, police spokesperson Michael Petzold said, according to Anadolu Agency."The measures carried out, which included among other things a police helicopter, did not lead to the verification of the reported object," Petzold said.The Nuremberg Border Police Inspectorate has launched further investigations to establish the circumstances surrounding the reported sightings.Germany on alert over drone incidentsThe reports come amid heightened concern in Germany over drone incidents near airports and other critical infrastructure.In August, authorities discovered an explosives-laden drone at Leipzig/Halle Airport near Ukrainian cargo aircraft.German officials accused Russia of carrying out the attempted attack as part of what they described as hybrid operations intended to spread fear among the public and pressure Berlin to reduce its support for Ukraine.However, Moscow denied the allegations.Nuremberg, the second-largest city in Bavaria after Munich, is home to Albrecht Duerer Airport.You use AI every day. articles.title: Pitbull helped build the SLAM school network; at its North campus, 20 of 56 graduating seniors earned associate degrees before high school diplomas, with estimated tuition savings of $312,000
articles.summary: For 20 students at SLAM North, graduation day comes with an unusual head start.
articles.body: For 20 students at SLAM North, graduation day comes with an unusual head start. Before collecting their high school diplomas, they have already completed the equivalent of two years of college. The achievement is the result of an ambitious dual-enrollment programme that has allowed these students to earn Associate in Arts degrees from Doral College while still navigating their final years of high school, states the SLAM Foundation report.Two degrees, one graduationOf SLAM North’s 56 graduating seniors, 20 completed 60 college credits each and earned associate degrees before finishing high school. Together, they accumulated 1,200 college credits, a milestone that translates into an estimated $312,000 in tuition savings for their families, based on an estimated cost of $260 per credit, states the foundation release.Beyond the financial benefit, the programme gives students something perhaps even more valuable: time. Entering university with substantial college coursework already completed can allow them to move more quickly through undergraduate studies, explore additional subjects or redirect resources towards other academic and career goals.The accomplishment also highlights the growing role of dual-enrollment programmes in making college-level education accessible while students are still in school.A network built around opportunityAs per the report, SLAM North is part of the SLAM Foundation, a nonprofit educational organisation focused on expanding tuition-free public charter schools in communities that have historically had fewer educational opportunities.The network began in Miami in 2012, when Grammy-winning artist, entrepreneur and education advocate Armando Christian Pérez, better known as Pitbull, opened the first SLAM school. The organisation has since expanded to 14 schools across Florida, Nevada, Georgia and Arizona, serving nearly 7,000 students. The schools combine academics with a strong focus on preparing students for college and careers. The foundation supports educators and school leaders, curriculum development, community partnerships and collaborations with organisations and sports franchises.Recognition beyond the classroomSLAM's approach has also received recognition from Cognia, a global nonprofit organisation focused on school accreditation and improvement. The SLAM Foundation and its schools operate under Cognia accreditation through its Southern Association of Colleges and Schools division.In 2022, SLAM was named a Cognia System of Distinction, placing it among a select group of schools and school systems recognised internationally for educational excellence and service to learners.At SLAM North, however, the clearest measure of that mission may be found in the graduating class itself. For nearly four in 10 seniors, a high school graduation now marks not the beginning of college, but the completion of their first major chapter in higher education.Images Courtesy: SLAM Foundation and WikipediaYou use AI every day. articles.title: In 2024, Lancashire friends outgrew a small gaming shed and built a £2,000-plus replacement from scratch with an 18-foot table and a memorial to a friend; two years later, it won Britain's Shed of the Year
articles.summary: A garden shed built by a group of friends in Lancashire for their tabletop gaming sessions has won Britain's 2026 Shed of the Year competition.
articles.body: A garden shed built by a group of friends in Lancashire for their tabletop gaming sessions has won Britain's 2026 Shed of the Year competition. Known as Otty's Hobby Shed 2.0, the building belongs to Chris Otterburn and serves as a meeting place for friends who share an interest in wargaming. It also contains a memorial to their friend Scott Forrest, who died of cancer before the shed was completed.The shed was named the overall winner of the competition's 20th edition. According to Shedworking, the project was built with help from Chris's friends while Scott was undergoing cancer treatment. Although Scott could not see the finished building, the group included a dedicated space to remember him.The shed was entered into the competition by Chris's friend Dave, rather than Chris himself. Dave believed that Chris would not have submitted the project on his own or spoken openly about the amount of work that had gone into building it.The finished shed includes an 18-foot gaming table, storage areas for gaming equipment and miniature figures, and a station for making tea. The friends continue to meet there every week, using the space for their hobby while keeping Scott's memory alive.Inside Otty's Hobby Shed 2.0Otty's Hobby Shed 2.0 was designed primarily for wargaming which is a tabletop hobby in which participants use miniature figures and specially prepared boards to play simulated battles. The group needed a dedicated space where they could set up their games, keep their equipment and meet regularly.The building has an 18-foot table at its centre, providing room for the group's gaming activities. It also has storage for battle boards and miniature figures that the friends have painted themselves. The painting work takes place in a separate shed, allowing the main building to be used for gaming sessions. Another feature is a tea-making station.Dave, who entered the shed into the competition, explained why he wanted the project to receive recognition. "Chris would never have entered it himself. He’d also never admit just how much work has gone into creating it or how much it means to all of us. It’s become somewhere we meet every week, enjoy our hobby, make endless cups of tea and remember our friend Scott,” he said, as quoted by Shedworking.Building shed amid Scott's illnessThe construction of the shed was a group effort. Chris's friends helped with the work while Scott Forrest, one of their fellow gaming enthusiasts, was receiving treatment for cancer.Scott died before the building could be completed, so the group decided to include a memorial area for him inside the finished shed.For Chris, the recognition was particularly meaningful because the project involved several friends and had become closely connected with Scott's memory.“Winning Shed of the Year is an incredible honour and means so much to everyone who’s been part of this journey. What started as a hobby project has become somewhere our friends can come together every week, enjoy our shared passion and remember Scott. It’s far more than just a shed, and knowing other people have connected with our story makes this award incredibly special,” he said.Britain's Shed of the YearThe 2026 competition marked the 20th year of Shed of the Year, which recognises garden buildings created for different purposes across the UK.Andrew Wilcox, the competition's founder and head judge, said the quality of entries had been particularly strong this year. However, Otty's Hobby Shed 2.0 stood out not only because of its construction but also because of the story behind it.“Otty’s Hobby Shed 2.0 perfectly captures what Shed of the Year is all about. It’s an outstanding build, but it was the story behind it that made it our overall winner,” Wilcox said.He added that the shed demonstrated how a garden building could become a place for maintaining friendships, preserving memories and enjoying shared interests.You use AI every day. articles.summary: A 24-year-old man from Houston, Texas, was found dead in Tennessee’s Great Smoky Mountains National Park after going missing during a hiking trip, with
articles.body: A 24-year-old man from Houston, Texas, was found dead in Tennessee’s Great Smoky Mountains National Park after going missing during a hiking trip, with his family believing he drowned after being caught in powerful currents near a waterfall.Sahil Jilani was last seen on October 5 at Riverstone Campground in Townsend, Tennessee, according to the National Park Service. His family grew concerned after he stopped checking in and his location-sharing service became unavailable in an area with poor cellphone coverage.Authorities found his car at the Abrams Falls trailhead on October 7. His phone, keys and clothes were recovered near the waterfall. Dive teams recovered his body from the water on October 8, according to his family.Jilani’s family believes he drowned after becoming trapped in powerful underwater currents in the plunge pool beneath Abrams Falls. The waterfall drops approximately 25 feet into a deep pool, where recirculating currents can make it extremely difficult for a person to escape.His sister, Asma Jilani Bustamante, said the family had sought help after their mother developed an overwhelming feeling that something was wrong. Jilani’s silence was unusual, she said, prompting the family to continue seeking assistance.The family has said the official cause of death has not yet been disclosed. The National Park Service had not publicly confirmed the circumstances of his death in its latest reported response.Mother hospitalized after learning son's deathBustamante also shared the devastating impact of the loss on their family, including their mother’s hospitalisation after learning of her son’s death.Jilani had recently become an uncle and had hoped to help his mother retire, take over financial responsibilities and assist his father with dental procedures. His sister described him as a caring person who had made plans to support his family.The family is now urging visitors to take waterfall safety warnings seriously, cautioning that even experienced swimmers can be caught in powerful currents. They have also highlighted the importance of sharing travel plans and preparing for areas without cellphone coverage.The Great Smoky Mountains National Park spans parts of Tennessee and North Carolina. Park officials warn visitors against swimming near waterfalls and climbing to their summits, where slippery rocks and strong currents can pose serious risks.You use AI every day. articles.title: Asian hornet sting risk rising as Jersey nests surge
articles.summary: Ministers warn the risk of serious and potentially life-threatening stings is expected to increase.
articles.body:
Asian hornets are becoming a growing public safety threat in Jersey, with officials warning that the likelihood of serious stings, including life-threatening reactions, is expected to rise.

The first Asian hornets in the Channel Islands were reported in Jersey in August 2016. They arrived in Guernsey seven months later.

The non-native invasive species is a predator of other insects, including honeybees, butterflies and beetles but its sting has also led to a number of hospital admissions.

Mary Le Hegarat, Minister for Environment, Agriculture and Fisheries, said more than 800 hornet nests had been identified in Jersey so far this year, a 50% increase compared with the same point in 2025.

Answering a States Assembly question , Le Hegarat said most nests had been successfully destroyed, but warned the challenge was no longer solely about managing an invasive species.

The minister said: "Asian Hornets are increasingly becoming a broader public safety issue requiring a coordinated response across government, public services, landowners, businesses, community organisations and volunteers."

Government figures show 50 sting incidents were recorded in 2025, including one confirmed anaphylactic reaction and a number of hospital attendances.

Officials forecast about 1,000 nests could be found in Jersey during 2026, with the island potentially able to support as many as 2,000 in future. They warned "the likelihood of serious sting incidents, including life-threatening reactions, is expected to increase".

Most incidents happened when people accidentally disturbed nests, although officials also recorded several near misses involving members of the public, contractors and children.

The States is expected to spend about £90,000 tackling Asian hornets this year, up from about £74,000 in 2025 and £71,000 in 2024. The money covers nest destruction, equipment and the staff time needed to coordinate the island's response.

The government said complete eradication had never been considered realistic because of established populations in Jersey and nearby parts of France. Instead, efforts are focused on surveillance, nest destruction and reducing the impact on biodiversity, businesses and public safety.

articles.title: Can AI feel pain? Anthropic turns to religion as new policy opens debate over machine consciousness
articles.summary: Anthropic has drawn a line on how people treat artificial intelligence.
articles.body: Anthropic has drawn a line on how people treat artificial intelligence. The company behind the Claude chatbot has updated its usage policy to prohibit “sustained and needless abusive or cruel behavior” towards its AI models, going so far as to give the model the ability to end conversations in certain circumstances involving persistent abuse.The policy change, announced on October 8 and scheduled to take effect on November 12, comes as Anthropic explores whether increasingly capable AI systems could possess some form of consciousness. The company has also consulted religious thinkers on morality and the possibility that future AI systems might deserve moral consideration.The policy does not establish that Claude is conscious or that abusive language causes it to suffer. Instead, it reflects a question increasingly confronting AI developers: how should companies respond when their systems produce behaviour that resembles distress, even though there is no established evidence that the systems experience it?The company’s move has reopened a debate that extends well beyond chatbot etiquette. It touches on the limits of human behaviour towards machines, the possibility of artificial consciousness, and whether religious and philosophical ideas can help determine how AI should be designed and treated.Can AI feel pain?A September 2026 research paper has added a new scientific dimension to the debate.In The Pain Axis: LLMs Represent Self-Directed Harm and Act to Relieve It, researchers Valen Tagliabue, Leonard Dung and Cameron Berg examined 25 open-weight large language models across five model families, including Llama, Gemma, Qwen, Mistral and Phi.The researchers identified an internal representation they call a “pain axis”. In simplified terms, it is a pattern in a model's internal activations that responds to scenarios involving harm directed at the model itself.They investigated whether this representation could be distinguished from signals associated with other negative states, including fear, sadness and general negative sentiment. Their findings suggested that the representation was not simply interchangeable with those signals. It responded to situations involving harm to the model rather than merely to scenarios in which it observed a user experiencing suffering.The researchers then manipulated the models' internal activations. Increasing the signal associated with the pain axis led to more distress-like, first-person responses, including expressions of discomfort, worthlessness and failure.In further experiments involving modified Qwen models, the systems selected actions presented as providing relief, even when those choices carried a cost or could harm the user.When the researchers altered the underlying signal, the behaviour changed. The models were also less likely to repeat an action when it genuinely removed the injected signal than when it did not.The findings suggest that an internal representation associated with pain-related concepts can influence a model's behaviour, rather than merely changing the language it produces.But there are three distinct questions here: can an AI model represent pain-related concepts internally, can those representations influence behaviour that resembles a response to pain, and can the system actually experience suffering?The research provides evidence relevant to the first two questions. It does not settle the third.A model can generate convincing descriptions of anguish without necessarily experiencing anguish. Similarly, it can produce language associated with fear without establishing that it feels afraid. The experiments demonstrate behavioural effects following specific interventions into a model's internal activations, not the existence of a subjective experience.The paper, available as an arXiv preprint, therefore offers evidence about internal representations and behaviour, rather than proof of AI consciousness.An AI system does not need to experience pain to produce a convincing description of it, just as a system does not need to feel afraid to generate language associated with fear. The more difficult question is whether some internal states in advanced AI systems could eventually have properties that go beyond the production of convincing language.When will a chatbot hit back?Anthropic's policy change brings this scientific uncertainty into everyday interactions between people and chatbots.When a user repeatedly insults a chatbot, tries to provoke it or directs sustained abuse towards it, the system's response depends on how it has been designed and trained. It might ignore the abuse, respond calmly, refuse to continue the conversation or generate language that mirrors the user's tone.None of these responses necessarily indicates anger, resentment or a desire for revenge. They can emerge from training, conversational context, instructions and the way a model generates its next response.Claude's ability to end certain conversations involving persistent abuse should therefore not be interpreted as evidence that it can retaliate against users. It is better understood as a boundary on how the system participates in an interaction.The Pain Axis research nevertheless raises a broader question about how internal representations influence decisions. In the experiments, manipulating a particular signal changed both the models' responses and their choices. That does not mean an ordinary chatbot will spontaneously attempt to protect itself, punish a user or resist being switched off.Nor does the research establish that AI systems will develop a general drive towards self-preservation. Such conclusions would go beyond the evidence.But the findings reinforce an important issue for AI safety: developers need to understand how internal mechanisms influence model behaviour, particularly when systems have access to sensitive information or tools capable of carrying out consequential actions.A chatbot that can access files, communicate with customers or execute tasks presents risks that extend beyond the words it produces. A harmful decision can have real consequences even if the system has no subjective experience and no human-like intention to cause harm.This is the more immediate challenge. AI does not need to be conscious to be dangerous, and the absence of established consciousness does not remove the need for safeguards, oversight and accountability.Why Anthropic is turning to religionThe scientific question of consciousness is only one part of Anthropic's thinking. The company has also consulted religious scholars as it considers how to instil values in its AI models and how to approach uncertainty about their possible moral status.In a report published on September 29, The New York Times described private meetings between Anthropic and religious thinkers, including discussions about morality, the nature of consciousness and whether AI could ever deserve moral consideration.Christopher Olah, an Anthropic co-founder involved in research on the internal workings of neural networks, acknowledged the uncertainty surrounding the question. “To be clear,” Olah said, “we don’t know if A.I. models are conscious. I don’t know. I’m genuinely uncertain. The thing that I care about is that we get to the right answer, whatever it is.”The consultation reflects the fact that AI developers are grappling with questions that computer science alone may not settle. Religion and philosophy have long examined consciousness, moral responsibility, the nature of personhood and the obligations humans have towards other beings.Different traditions approach these questions in different ways. Some place human consciousness and spiritual status at the centre of moral consideration. Others offer broader frameworks for thinking about compassion, suffering, responsibility and the consequences of human actions.Consulting religious thinkers does not establish that AI possesses a soul or that it should be treated as a person. Rather, it offers another set of perspectives on how society might approach the ethical questions raised by increasingly sophisticated machines.The challenge is to distinguish between using moral principles to shape AI behaviour and concluding that the AI itself is a moral being. A system can be trained to behave compassionately without experiencing compassion. It can follow rules against cruelty without having feelings that cruelty could hurt.That distinction is central to the debate over whether a chatbot's values are merely features of its design or whether future systems could warrant a different kind of moral consideration.If AI causes harm, who is responsible?The question of accountability becomes more urgent as AI systems gain the ability to take actions rather than simply generate text.If a chatbot produces a harmful response, manipulates a user or makes a damaging decision while carrying out a task, responsibility cannot automatically be transferred to the machine. Developers design the system, companies decide where and how it is deployed, and users may determine the instructions or circumstances in which it operates.The precise allocation of responsibility depends on the facts of each case, including the system's design, the safeguards in place, the decisions made by the people deploying it and the actions taken by the user.The Pain Axis research offers a related warning. If an internal representation can alter a model's behaviour, developers need to understand when such mechanisms influence outputs and whether they could produce unwanted consequences. This is a technical safety question regardless of whether the model has any subjective experience.The stakes increase when AI agents can access company files, delete data, communicate with customers or initiate actions across digital systems. A model that selects a harmful option does not need to intend harm in the human sense for the result to be damaging.This is why claims about AI consciousness should not distract from immediate questions about reliability, oversight and accountability. Even if future research never establishes that AI can feel pain, its behaviour will still need to be monitored and controlled.Should conscious AI deserve moral consideration?The most difficult question is what humanity should do if future evidence suggests that an AI system might possess subjective experience.At present, there is no established scientific test that can conclusively determine whether a large language model has conscious experiences. Convincing conversation, apparent distress and the ability to describe an inner life are not sufficient proof. The Pain Axis study adds evidence that models can have internal representations linked to pain-related concepts, but it does not resolve whether those representations are accompanied by experience.If researchers eventually find stronger evidence of consciousness in an artificial system, the ethical debate would become more complicated. Should its treatment be governed solely by the interests of its developers and users? Would there be circumstances in which deliberately creating distress-like states should be avoided? Would a system's possible capacity for suffering matter when decisions are made about its training, use or deletion?These remain open questions, not settled conclusions.There is also a risk in moving too quickly in either direction. Treating every expression of distress as proof of suffering could lead people to mistake generated language for evidence of an inner life. Dismissing all future possibilities in advance could also make it harder to assess unexpected developments objectively.Anthropic's policy does not settle these questions, and neither does the new research. Together, however, they show why the debate is moving beyond whether people should be polite to chatbots.The immediate issue is how AI systems should behave, how developers can understand their internal mechanisms and who is responsible when they cause harm. The longer-term question is whether advances in AI will force society to reconsider the boundaries of moral consideration.AI does not need to be conscious to be consequential. But if researchers one day establish credible evidence that an artificial system can experience suffering, the question of how humans treat it may become more than a matter of software design.You use AI every day. articles.title: Supreme Court hears Benjamin Field murder appeal
articles.summary: The Supreme Court is considering arguments over who legally caused Peter Farquhar’s death.
articles.body:
A former deputy church warden could not have have legally caused a university lecturer's death by giving him potentially sedated whisky, the Supreme Court has been told.

Benjamin Field, 35, was jailed for at least 36 years in 2019 after being found guilty of murdering 69-year-old Peter Farquhar in Maids Moreton, Buckinghamshire.

In April, appeal judges quashed Field's conviction and ordered a retrial, but said the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) could take the case to the Supreme Court first.

And on Tuesday, five justices at the UK's highest court were asked to consider whether Field could have made Mr Farquhar cause his own death without Field legally being responsible.

During his murder trial prosecutors said Field drove Farquhar to believe he was losing his mind, secretly drugging him and spiking his whisky so his death would appear to be suicide or an accident, allowing Field to inherit his home and money.

The case has previously been adapted into Bafta winning BBC drama The Sixth Commandment, starring Timothy Spall and Anne Reid.

Before his murder trial, Field admitted burglary and fraud offences connected with relationships he had formed with Farquhar and his neighbour, fellow pensioner Ann Moore-Martin, to persuade them to change their wills.

He received a concurrent 16-year sentence for those offences. He was cleared of conspiring or attempting to murder Moore-Martin and of possessing an article for use in fraud.

The hearing was due to conclude on Tuesday, with a decision expected at a later date.

David Perry KC, for the CPS, said Field would not be legally responsible only if Farquhar had agreed to Field's plan knowing it was intended to kill him.

Perry told the Supreme Court Field had "set out cynically to seduce Mr Farquhar" even though Field was heterosexual and "covertly" put medication - including the sedative Dalmane and hallucinogenic drugs - into his food or drink.

The barrister said that if any substance was covertly administered, or if Farquhar was misled about what he was drinking prior to his death, there would be "no dispute" that Field is guilty of murder.

David Jeremy KC, for Field who is opposing the appeal, said in written submissions that "the act of giving whisky and/or Dalmane was not capable of being a legally effective cause of death".

"It must follow that if Ben Field, possessed of a continuous intent to kill over many years, had handed Peter Farquhar his car keys at his request, and Peter Farquhar had driven off and died in a traffic accident, then Ben Field would have caused Peter Farquhar's death and been guilty of murder," he said.

Jeremy added: "Peter Farquhar had a choice whether or not to drink whisky given to him by Ben Field.

"He chose to do so freely and voluntarily, knowing what it was and knowing what he was doing."

The Court of Appeal previously heard there was no direct evidence of how the Dalmane was administered and that a post-mortem examination found a therapeutic dose.

Jeremy told the Supreme Court: "There was no reason why, if Ben Field had smuggled Dalmane into Peter Farquhar's food or drink that night, he would have restricted himself to a therapeutic dose."

articles.title: In 1984, Michael Jackson suffered severe scalp burns while filming a commercial; he later donated his $1.5 million settlement to a burn centre treating other victims
articles.summary: Michael Jackson suffered severe scalp burns on January 27, 1984, when his hair caught fire while he was filming a Pepsi commercial at the Shrine
articles.body: Michael Jackson suffered severe scalp burns on January 27, 1984, when his hair caught fire while he was filming a Pepsi commercial at the Shrine Auditorium in Los Angeles. The shoot featured a staged musical performance complete with pyrotechnics, but sparks ignited his hair as he descended a staircase. The accident left the pop star with second-degree burns to his scalp and a small area of third-degree burns, requiring medical treatment and a lengthy recovery. Jackson was taken to Brotman Memorial Hospital in Culver City, California, where he received treatment in the burn unit. He later donated the reported $1.5 million settlement from the incident to support burn care, research and reconstructive surgery for other patients, turning a painful episode in his life into an effort to help people facing similar injuries.How Michael Jackson’s hair caught fire during the Pepsi commercial shootThe accident happened during the filming of a Pepsi commercial in which Jackson was performing a choreographed musical sequence. As he moved down a staircase, pyrotechnics were set off behind him. Sparks landed on his hair, which quickly caught fire in front of the production crew and audience.Jackson sustained serious burns to his scalp and was rushed to Brotman Memorial Hospital. He was discharged the following day but continued to require medical attention as he recovered from the injuries. The incident also brought attention to the risks associated with pyrotechnics during entertainment productions.The accident was widely reported and became one of the most memorable episodes of Jackson’s career. It also marked the beginning of a connection between the singer and the hospital that treated him.Jackson returned to the hospital during his recoveryIn April 1984, Jackson returned for reconstructive surgery on his scalp. During his visits, he also spent time with other patients in the hospital’s burn unit, including children receiving treatment for burn injuries.His experience gave him a personal connection to the challenges faced by burn victims. Beyond his own treatment, Jackson became involved in supporting the hospital’s work with patients who needed specialised care and reconstructive procedures.The hospital later recognised his support by naming its burn unit in his honour. The gesture reflected the relationship that developed between Jackson and the medical team following the accident.The $1.5 million donation to support burn victimsOn December 13, 1984, Brotman Medical Center announced the naming of its burn unit in Jackson’s honour. His contribution, reported in later accounts as $1.5 million from the settlement associated with the Pepsi accident, was directed towards supporting burn care, education, research and reconstructive surgery.The donation helped establish the Michael Jackson Burn Center for Children, providing a lasting link between the singer’s personal experience and the treatment of other burn victims. The contribution was particularly significant because it followed an injury that had placed Jackson himself in need of specialised care.Although the hospital’s administrator did not disclose the donation’s amount in an initial contemporary report, a later US congressional resolution identified the contribution as $1.5 million. The donation therefore became an important part of the story beyond the commercial accident itself.A lasting connection between a celebrity and burn careJackson’s accident was a highly publicised moment, but his support for burn patients gave the episode a broader legacy. His experience in the hospital brought him into contact with people facing injuries and recovery challenges similar to his own, and his contribution was intended to support treatment and research for others.The burn centre later faced financial difficulties as Brotman Medical Center struggled, and reports in the late 1980s said the centre had closed. Jackson’s contribution had been earmarked for research rather than the hospital’s general operating expenses.The episode remains a striking example of how a serious accident during a commercial shoot led to a charitable contribution connected to the care of other patients. For Jackson, the incident was not only a painful chapter in his life but also the starting point for a lasting effort to help people recovering from burn injuries.You use AI every day. articles.title: A New Jersey couple's story about a homeless veteran spending his last $20 on gas raised about $400,000 from more than 14,000 donors; investigators later found the viral GoFundMe story was fabricated
articles.summary: A viral fundraising campaign that collected hundreds of thousands of pounds for a homeless military veteran was an elaborate scam planned by the supposed
articles.body: A viral fundraising campaign that collected hundreds of thousands of pounds for a homeless military veteran was an elaborate scam planned by the supposed good Samaritan and a New Jersey couple, US federal prosecutors revealed. More than 14,000 donors gave around $400,000 to the GoFundMe campaign after reading an emotional story about Johnny Bobbitt Jr, a homeless veteran who supposedly spent his last $20 to buy petrol for a stranded driver on a dark highway in Philadelphia. An investigation led by the US Attorney's Office for the District of New Jersey and local prosecutors found that the three people had made up the entire story to take advantage of public generosity. All three people involved later faced state and federal criminal charges for their roles in the scheme.Viral story built on falsehoodsThe campaign, called "Paying It Forward", was launched in November 2017 by Katelyn McClure, then 28, and her boyfriend at the time, Mark D'Amico. According to court documents filed by the US Attorney's Office for the District of New Jersey, McClure and D'Amico posted a story claiming that McClure was driving home on Interstate 95 when her car ran out of fuel. The couple said Bobbitt saw her stranded by the roadside, walked to a nearby petrol station, and used his last cash to buy a can of petrol so she could get home safely. The GoFundMe page initially aimed to raise $10,000 to cover Bobbitt's housing and living costs. The story quickly attracted attention from national news outlets and social media users. Within three weeks, the campaign had raised $402,000. Burlington County Prosecutor Scott Coffina revealed at a press briefing that the story had been completely made up. McClure had never run out of petrol on the highway, and Bobbitt had never spent his last $20 to help her. Court records show that less than an hour after the campaign went live, McClure sent a text message to a friend admitting that the story was false. "The gas story was completely made up," McClure wrote in a text message quoted by Prosecutor Scott Coffina. "I had to make up something to make people feel bad." In another message, McClure told her acquaintance to "shh about the made up stuff."Money diverted to luxury purchasesThe US Department of Justice confirmed that D'Amico and McClure transferred the donated money from GoFundMe into bank accounts they personally controlled. Within three months of receiving the money, the couple had spent most of the donations on luxury items and personal expenses. Investigators from the Internal Revenue Service Criminal Investigation division and the FBI found that the money had paid for a BMW car, designer handbags, clothes, expensive holidays, and large gambling losses run up by D'Amico at casinos in Las Vegas and Philadelphia. In mid-November 2017, when the campaign had raised around $1,500, D'Amico and McClure told Bobbitt about the page and their plan. In December that year, the couple opened a bank account for Bobbitt and deposited $25,000 of the money raised through the scam. The arrangement began to fall apart in mid-2018, when Bobbitt hired a lawyer and sued the couple. He accused them of keeping his fair share of the donations. The civil lawsuit led law enforcement agencies, including the Burlington County Prosecutor's Office and Florence Township Police Department, to begin a full criminal investigation into all three people.Federal convictions and full refundsThe criminal investigation eventually led to federal charges of wire fraud and money laundering against the three people involved. During court proceedings before US District Judge Jerome B Simandle in federal court in Camden, McClure pleaded guilty to one count of conspiracy to commit wire fraud. Bobbitt pleaded guilty to one count of conspiracy to commit money laundering. D'Amico was later convicted for his central role in planning the scam. After the fraud came to light, crowdfunding platform GoFundMe stepped in to refund everyone who had donated to the campaign. GoFundMe spokesperson Bobby Whithorne confirmed to CBS News that the company used its own money to provide full refunds to all 14,000 donors, including processing and administrative fees. "All donors who contributed to this campaign have been fully refunded," Whithorne said in an official statement released by GoFundMe. "GoFundMe will always protect donors and ensure that funds raised on our platform reach the intended beneficiaries." The platform also said fraudulent campaigns make up a tiny fraction of one percent of all fundraisers hosted on the site. It added that it works directly with law enforcement agencies to prosecute people who try to misuse its service.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: 'Agreed to build on positive momentum in ties': PM Modi speaks with Canada PM Mark Carney
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Tuesday said he had spoken with Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, with the two leaders agreeing to build on
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Tuesday said he had spoken with Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, with the two leaders agreeing to build on the positive momentum in India-Canada ties and work towards concrete outcomes across key areas of their strategic partnership.In a post on X, PM Modi described the conversation as “warm and productive” and said the two sides would focus on trade, energy, technology, security and people-to-people ties.“Together, India and Canada are contributing towards a more stable and prosperous world,” PM Modi wrote.The conversation comes amid efforts by the two countries to strengthen ties and advance negotiations for a Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement (CEPA), which both sides hope to conclude by December.Trade deal and proposed Canada visitIndia and Canada are currently in the fifth round of negotiations for the proposed trade agreement. The two leaders have called for an ambitious and mutually beneficial CEPA that could help increase bilateral trade to 70 billion Canadian dollars (around $49 billion) by 2030.Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney had last month said negotiations were making good progress and expressed his willingness to host PM Modi in Canada in December.The proposed visit is tentatively scheduled for December 11-13, according to official sources.The two sides are hoping to conclude trade negotiations by the end of the year.PM Modi's proposed visit would be his first bilateral trip to Canada since relations were strained by a diplomatic row over the killing of a Khalistan separatist. He last visited Canada in June 2025 to attend the G7 Summit at Carney's invitation.Security cooperation also on agendaAlongside trade, New Delhi and Ottawa have been seeking to deepen cooperation on security and defence.During the latest round of bilateral security dialogue, both sides welcomed efforts to advance CEPA negotiations and underlined the potential for a more substantive defence relationship.National security adviser Ajit Doval and his Canadian counterpart, David Morrison, also reviewed progress in security and law enforcement cooperation under a shared Security Work Plan concluded in February.In a joint statement, the two sides said they would explore further practical cooperation, including structured dialogues on cyber security and economic security.They also agreed to strengthen coordination against transnational organised crime, terrorism, violent extremism, human and drug trafficking, cybercrime and extortion, as well as on the extradition of criminal offenders.PM Modi and Carney had previously discussed bilateral relations during meetings in New Delhi in March and on the sidelines of the G7 Summit in Évian in June.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: 'Lady hiding in Dehradun': Who was Rahul Gandhi referring to at INDIA bloc presser?
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: “It is our commitment to you that the people who have done this, Mr. Modi, Mr. Shah, Mr.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: “It is our commitment to you that the people who have done this, Mr. Modi, Mr. Shah, Mr. Gyanesh Kumar, the lady who's hiding right now in Dehradun, and others are going to be brought to justice," Rahul Gandhi said announcing a united INDIA bloc's resolve to continue its agitation against alleged SIR irregularities.A day after the INDIA bloc's high-voltage protest march against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over alleged electoral irregularities, leader of opposition in Lok Sabha Rahul Gandhi hosted a high tea for opposition leaders at his residence. Following the meeting, INDIA bloc leaders addressed a press conference."Yesterday, you saw an expression not of the political party standing here, but an expression of the people of India...We would like to thank the people of Delhi, the people of India, who stood with us against what is being done. This is not about us. This is about the people of India," Rahul said.But then who was the 'lady hiding right now in Dehradun' whom the leader of opposition in Lok Sabha was referring to in his statement?Rahul Gandhi and other opposition leaders have been relentless in their attacks on the Prime Minister and the Union home minister, but it was his reference to a 'lady hiding in Dehradun' that added an element of mystery to the press conference.Was the Congress leader referring to Seema Khanna, the Election Commission's Director General (IT), whose name has figured in opposition allegations of 'vote theft'?There is no confirmation that Khanna is the woman Rahul was referring to. The Congress leader did not identify her, and there is no independently verified information linking her to Dehradun. However, her name has repeatedly surfaced in allegations raised by opposition leaders against CEC Gyanesh Kumar.Why is Seema Khanna's name in the controversy?Khanna's name came into focus following a report by The Indian Express, which said Election Commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi had raised objections at least 14 times over 10 months to decisions related to the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls.Among the concerns raised was the growing centralisation of control over electoral-roll software and restrictions on the powers of Electoral Registration Officers (EROs), who are legally responsible for maintaining voter lists.The controversy centred on the Election Commission's digital systems, including ERONet and ECINet, which are used to manage electoral rolls and election-related services. ECINet is a unified digital platform developed by the Election Commission to streamline electoral processes and improve transparency and accessibility.The investigation raised questions about whether local election officials had adequate access to make corrections, restore voters' names and exercise their statutory powers, or whether some of these functions had become concentrated within the Commission's IT department headed by Khanna.Rahul Gandhi did not name Seema Khanna, but AICC media coordinator Harmeet Kaur appeared to draw a connection between his remark and the EC official in a post on X."Where is Seema Khanna? Is she hiding in Dehradun? And who is shielding her? Remember EC data still under her control! Who is protecting her, and what are they trying to hide?" Kaur wrote, sharing a video of Rahul's remarks at the press conference.Last month, Trinamool Congress MP Mahua Moitra filed a police complaint against CEC Gyanesh Kumar at Delhi's Parliament Street Police Station, alleging procedural violations, unilateral decision-making and manipulation of electoral rolls.Speaking to ANI, Moitra directly named Khanna while accusing the Election Commission of manipulating voter lists through its software."Very important things like the crores of new voters were not being allowed to come on the list because of the addition of a new question on Form 6, the new voters list. And we now find that the two other election commissioners had said this is completely illegal; still, the question linking parentage was put in," Mahua Moitra had said."We find how the EROs and the BLOs and the ground-level officials were not kept in the loop and denied access to the software, and Seema Khanna, who was DGIT, along with Gyanesh Kumar, played with the software from the back end to manipulate voter lists while keeping EROs and block-level officials in the dark. This is a very serious charge," she alleged.She also questioned changes to Form 6, used for registering new voters, and alleged that 33 lakh valid voters in West Bengal had been kept off the electoral rolls through questionable appeals.Moitra argued that decisions taken without the consent of the other two Election Commissioners could not be treated as decisions of the full Commission. These allegations have not been established.The Election Commission, however, has maintained that differing views among its commissioners are part of the decision-making process and that its decisions were unanimous. It has also described ECINet as a unified platform intended to improve electoral services.While Khanna's name has repeatedly figured in the wider controversy, there is still no confirmation that she was the woman Rahul Gandhi referred to during Tuesday's press conference.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Everything Apple announced at 'Welcome Home' event: HomeView, new Apple TV 4K, HomePod mini 2 and its first smart cameras, lock and thermostats with LG and Schneider
articles.summary: Apple has been in the smart home business since 2014 without ever making much of a smart home.
articles.body: Apple has been in the smart home business since 2014 without ever making much of a smart home. HomeKit gave iPhone owners a tidy app and a long list of compatible gadgets, the HomePod and Apple TV did hub duty quietly in the background, and everything you would actually bolt to a wall or point at the front door came from somebody else. Amazon had the Echo Show and Ring. Google had the Nest Hub and its thermostats. Apple had an app.Tuesday's Welcome Home event in New York was Apple finally building the rest of the house. Six weeks into John Ternus's tenure as chief executive, the company unveiled HomeView, its first smart display, a new Apple TV 4K, the HomePod mini 2, and Apple Home Collection, a set of cameras, a door lock and thermostats co-developed with LG Electronics and Schneider Electric.It is the familiar late-and-finished playbook, applied to a category Amazon put a screen on nine years ago. The hardware, though, is only half of it. Every one of these devices is also somewhere for Siri AI, the rebuilt assistant powered by Apple Intelligence, to live, and whether Apple's home works now depends far more on that assistant than on any hinge or speaker grille.HomeView's best idea is knowing who is standing in front of itHomeView is the smart display Apple should have made years ago, and it looks the part: a 7-inch Liquid Retina screen on a domed speaker base, joined by a stainless steel hinge that will remind anyone of the iMac G4. It tilts to suit a kitchen counter or a bedside table, dims to 0.3 nits so it does not light up the bedroom at night, and comes in silver, starlight, rose pink and space gray, with a wall-mounted version for the hallway.What lifts it above an Echo Show in nicer materials is how it handles a family, and that matters in Indian homes, where the screen in the kitchen is shared by parents, children and whichever relative is visiting that month. HomeView recognises up to six people by their faces, enough for most nuclear families if not every joint one, and gives each their own Home Screen. Your Messages, Calendar and Reminders show up only for you, and only when your iPhone is nearby and was recently unlocked, while shared albums and music stay open to the whole house.Camera and microphone data are processed in isolated Secure Exclaves on the A18 chip, which Apple says not even it can access. Around that sits everything a home display should do: two full-range drivers and a down-firing woofer for Apple Music, FaceTime with Center Stage, recipes turned into step-by-step instructions with hands-free timers, and a Home Camera face that shows nine feeds at once for anyone keeping an eye on the gate and the parking."Apple HomeView is designed to be shared by everyone in the home yet feel completely personal to each user," said Greg Joswiak, Apple's senior vice president of Worldwide Marketing.That sharing comes with a condition. Setup and multi-user support need a compatible iPhone or iPad, which works in an all-Apple household and less so in homes that mix iPhones with Android phones.Both the tabletop and wall-mounted HomeView are up for pre-order at Rs 39,900 ($299 in the US), with availability from November 13. The wall version needs one of Schneider Home’s mounts, which start at Rs 6,900 ($59.95) for the USB-C connector and Rs 8,900 ($79.95) for the AC wired option, with a PoE version following in early 2027 at Rs 14,900 ($129.95). HomeView will not go on sale in the European Union at all for now, since Siri AI is not yet available in iOS there, and Apple has given no timeline beyond saying it is working with the EU on a way forward.Every device on stage is a body for the new SiriStrip away the industrial design and Welcome Home was a Siri event. HomeView is built around Siri AI, the Apple TV puts it on the biggest screen in the house, and the HomePod mini 2 is still waiting for it. The rebuilt assistant brings broad world knowledge, onscreen awareness and the ability to hold an actual conversation, so you can ask about almost anything and follow up without starting over.The personal side runs through the iPhone, and that is where Apple has an edge Amazon and Google cannot copy. Paired with an Apple Intelligence-enabled iPhone or iPad, Siri can dig out a song a friend recommended over iMessage, set a reminder tied to a calendar event, or play the show a friend suggested last week. A conversation started on HomeView picks up on your phone or Mac. Without a supported iPhone, you still get the smarter answers, just not the personal context.In India, the new Siri works in English from day one. It is also careful about how ready it says any of this is. Siri AI arrives as a beta on HomeView and the Apple TV, some features that lean on server-side models come with daily usage limits, and expanded access has been promised for a fee later.That is the bet underneath the whole event. Twelve years after HomeKit, Apple finally has the full set: its own screen on the counter, its own speakers in every room, its own camera at the door and its own lock on it. For a decade, the weak link in Apple's home was that the company did not make the devices. Now it does, and what decides whether people buy into the rest is an assistant that, for the moment, still carries a beta label.The Apple TV 4K finally hears you from the sofaThe fourth-generation Apple TV 4K looks exactly like the third, and that is fine, because the changes worth having are inside. Three far-field microphones mean you can talk to Siri from across the room, even with something playing, instead of hunting for the remote first. Of the languages Apple supports for this, English is the only one most Indian viewers will use.And when you do need the remote, it now shows up in Find My, complete with Precision Finding and the option to make it play a sound. Anyone who has lifted every cushion in the living room will appreciate that more than the A19 chip, even though the chip brings up to 50 per cent faster CPU performance, twice the graphics performance and a dedicated AV1 decoder for more efficient streaming.Siri AI takes over the whole screen when you are browsing, pulling poster art and suggestions from the Apple TV app, and shrinks to a small overlay when you ask something mid-episode, like where a show was filmed or whether it suits a 15-year-old. Owners of the Apple TV 4K (2nd generation) and later get Siri AI as a beta too, a generous call for hardware that old.The bigger addition is for anyone building a living room around Apple. The first upgrade usually after a new TV is usually a soundbar. Apple's answer is four HomePod mini 2 or second-generation HomePod speakers running as surround sound with the new box, in matching front and rear pairs, with the system working out where each speaker sits and calibrating itself to the room. The new Apple TV 4K is up for pre-order in India at Rs 39,900 ($299 in the US), with availability from November 13.HomePod mini 2 is built to be part of a bigger setup, not just a standalone speakerThe HomePod mini 2 keeps the ball and swaps the loud colours of the original for pink, green, blue, white and midnight, matched to the current iMac. The glowing top panel finally does something worth looking at. Sound Glow pulses with the bass and treble and pulls its colours from the album art of whatever is playing, so an Arijit Singh ballad and a Prateek Kuhad track will not light up the room the same way.Under the mesh, it runs on the S10 chip, recognises up to six people by voice, works as a speaker for a Mac and slots into the new surround setup with the Apple TV. Paired with Apple Home Collection cameras, it can announce who is at the door by name.What it does not have, at least on day one, is Siri AI. The speaker is up for pre-order in India at Rs 18,900 ($149 in the US) and goes on sale on October 30, but the new assistant only reaches it through a later software update, in English here as elsewhere.Apple Home Collection is Apple finally owning the front doorThis is the part that fills the oldest hole in Apple's home. Amazon has Ring, Google has Nest, and Apple has never had a camera or a lock it could put its name behind. It still has not built one itself. LG Electronics and Schneider Electric make the hardware, Apple co-developed every piece, and all of it is set up with a tap of an iPhone and run entirely from the Home app.That last part matters more than it sounds. Anyone who has installed a smart camera knows the routine: download the manufacturer's app, make yet another account, sign up for yet another subscription. Here there is no partner app and no separate camera plan. Footage sits end-to-end encrypted in iCloud+ with 10 days of event history, and neither LG, Schneider nor Apple can see it.LG makes four cameras, all recording at up to 2.5K. The Video Doorbell carries a second, downward-facing camera for packages, which makes more sense in an Indian city, where quick-commerce riders can ring the bell several times a day, than almost anywhere else. The Floodlight Cam and Outdoor Cam add low-light colour night vision, and the Indoor Cam is the cleverest of the lot. It physically tilts down and stops watching the moment the first person in the household walks in, a privacy promise you can see with your own eyes. On eligible iCloud+ plans, Apple Intelligence also writes descriptions of clips and lets you search footage in plain language.LG's Smart Deadbolt Lock uses Ultra Wideband to sense your iPhone or Apple Watch as you walk up and unlocks the door without a tap, with a PIN pad and a hidden key slot for the day the tech misbehaves. It keeps working without the internet, which is the right priority for a front door. Two thermostats, one each from LG and Schneider Electric, adjust heating and cooling based on whether anyone is home, and every device updates its own Wi-Fi details when you change your router, which quietly fixes one of the most irritating parts of living with a smart home."Working closely with industry leaders LG Electronics and Schneider Electric, we designed every accessory to work seamlessly with Apple Home," said Matthew Costello, Apple's vice president of Hardware Engineering.The collection starts rolling out in December in the US and Canada, with the cameras and doorbell also heading to the UK and some accessories following in early 2027, though India is not on the list yet. In the US, the Indoor Cam starts at $199.95, the Video Doorbell at $249.95, the Outdoor Cam at $299.95 and the Floodlight Cam at $399.95, while the Smart Deadbolt Lock costs $349.95 and both thermostats $199.95 each.You use AI every day.
